title: Laird Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Laird wells have an 80 ft median depth, 15 gpm median yield, and estimated finished costs of $8,800-$16,400.
h1: Laird, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost Guide
intro_html:
If you are buying land or planning a home near Laird, the local well records give you a useful starting point. Within 5 miles, Colorado DWR records show 419 permitted wells. Of those, 243 are recorded as constructed, 276 report total depth, 118 report pump yield, and 24 report static water level.

This is a plains setting with alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. The records include both unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer wells and Ogallala wells. Neighboring wells are helpful evidence, but they do not guarantee the same result on your lot. Permit history, well construction, water rights, septic layout, and the intended use all need to be checked before you commit to a property.

sections.heading: Laird wells are usually shallow, but the lot still matters
sections.html:
The median recorded well depth near Laird is 80 feet. The middle half runs from 50 to 120 feet, and 60% of the depth records are under 100 feet. The deepest well on record is 250 feet, while 40% fall in the 100-to-300-foot range. No recorded wells fall in the 300-to-600-foot or 600-plus-foot ranges.

For a drilling bid, that 50-to-120-foot middle range is more useful than the median alone. A contractor should price the expected depth, then explain how casing, grout, access, trenching, and an unexpected deeper hole would be handled. Laird's alluvium and plains sedimentary rock are different from fractured granite, but local changes in formation can still affect both depth and water production. Review nearby construction records instead of relying only on a countywide estimate.

sections.heading: Pump yields near Laird are generally workable for homes
sections.html:
The median reported pump yield is 15.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 10.0 and 25.0 gallons per minute. Among wells with yield records, 58% report more than 15 gallons per minute, 36% report 5 to 15 gallons per minute, and 5% report 1 to 5 gallons per minute. No reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute.

That distribution is encouraging for a typical household, but a pump test is not the same as guaranteed long-term supply. Ask for the well construction report, test method, and recovery information. A 10-gallon-per-minute result can serve a home differently from a 25-gallon-per-minute result if irrigation, livestock, storage, or multiple users are planned. Confirm the DWR permit's allowed use before assuming the well can support every proposed use.

sections.heading: Water levels show a useful local starting point
sections.html:
Only 24 wells report a static water level, so the water-level sample is much smaller than the depth sample. In those records, the median depth to water is 56 feet, with the middle half from 19 to 74 feet. That gives a buyer a practical starting point for pump and trench planning, but it is not a complete measurement of the water table across Laird.

The supplied records do not include a water-level series by decade, so they do not establish a dropping or rising trend. Seasonal conditions, pumping, well location, and the way a static level was measured can all matter. Before building, have a qualified contractor review the closest well logs and measure an existing well when possible. Keep the planned pump setting and pressure system separate from assumptions about static water level.

sections.heading: Permit history points to an established local drilling pattern
sections.html:
Laird's permit records span several decades, with 7 permits in the 1950s, 16 in the 1960s, 32 in the 1970s, 20 in the 1980s, 69 in the 1990s, 45 in the 2000s, 50 in the 2010s, and 21 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025. Domestic or household wells account for 49% of the use mix, and stock wells also account for 49%. Irrigation is listed on 15%, while monitoring accounts for 3%.

Wellstone Industries Dba Twiss & Wilson Drilling Inc. is the most common driller in the records, with 113 wells. Wellstone Services, LLC has 23, and Twiss, Aaron D. has 13. Those records can help you identify local construction patterns, but they are not a substitute for current bids and a site-specific review.

sections.heading: A Laird well budget starts around the local depth range
sections.html:
For Laird's alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, the supplied drilling model uses a typical rate of $35-$55 per foot. At the 80-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $2,800-$4,400. That is only the hole. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $8,800-$16,400.

The finished number is the figure to carry into a building budget. Confirm what each bid includes: casing and grout, drilling mobilization, pump size, pressure tank, controls, electrical work, water testing, trench length, and restoration. Access for the rig can also affect the proposal. If the site is outside the median depth range, the drilling portion may move materially. Get the contractor to state the assumed depth and the price treatment for additional footage before work starts.

sections.heading: Check water quality, septic space, and the permit before buying
sections.html:
Mapped environmental information within about 10 miles includes 11 PFAS sampling or contamination sites. There are no historic mine features and no EPA Superfund or cleanup sites in the supplied data. A mapped site does not prove that a particular well is contaminated, but it is a reason to test the water and ask for the location and status of nearby sampling. Test for the contaminants appropriate to the property and intended use.

Low yield, a dry hole, poor construction, and an unsuitable pump are separate risks. Check casing and grout records, well age, pump performance, and recent water tests. Keep the well, septic system, replacement area, driveway, and proposed house in a workable layout. Colorado DWR permits control the allowed use. Exempt household-use wells have a 35 gpm pumping limit, and an augmentation plan may be needed in an over-appropriated basin. Confirm the legal water supply before closing or building.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Laird, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded well depth within 5 miles of Laird is 80 feet. The middle half runs from 50 to 120 feet, and 60% are under 100 feet. The deepest recorded well is 250 feet. Use those figures to compare nearby logs, but have a driller price the specific lot because geology and access can change the result.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Laird?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $35-$55 per foot. At the 80-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $2,800-$4,400. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $8,800-$16,400. Ask what the bid includes and how additional footage, casing, grout, and difficult access are charged.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce near Laird?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield is 15.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half is 10.0-25.0 gallons per minute. The records show 58% above 15 gallons per minute, 36% from 5 to 15, and 5% from 1 to 5. These are reported well results, not a guarantee for a new well.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Laird?
faq.a: The records identify 11 PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles, but that does not establish contamination in a particular well. Test the property water before drinking it and ask for nearby sampling information. Review the well construction record and test for contaminants appropriate to the site, household, and intended use.

faq.q: What should I check before buying land with a well near Laird?
faq.a: Check the DWR permit, allowed use, construction report, pump yield, static water level, casing and grout, and recent water tests. The area includes domestic, stock, irrigation, and monitoring wells, so a permit's use matters. Also confirm septic setbacks and replacement space, building access, and whether an augmentation plan is required for the intended use.
